name: Arsa
title: Overseer of King Elah's house in Tirzah
summary: In the northern kingdom of Israel's turbulent early history, Arza played an unexpected role as the backdrop for a dramatic shift in power. He held the high title 'over the house' (Hebrew: al ha-bayit) and served as royal steward under King Elah in Tirzah. While Elah was drinking himself drunk in Arza's house, the army commander Zimri seized the opportunity to carry out his coup and struck down the king. Through this event, the prophet Jehu's prophecy of judgment against Baasha's dynasty was fulfilled, and Baasha's family line was completely wiped out. Arza is mentioned only in this single passage in 1 Kings, but his position sheds light on the administrative structures of the northern kingdom.

keyEvents.title: Zimri's coup in Arsa's house
keyEvents.description: King Elah drank himself drunk in the house of his overseer Arsa in Tirzah. Zimri, commander of half the chariots, took the opportunity to break in and kill the king. Arsa held the title 'over the house,' one of the highest administrative positions in the kingdom.

keyEvents.title: The fulfillment of the prophet Jehu's words
keyEvents.description: The murder of King Elah in Arsa's house marked the final fulfillment of the prophet Jehu's judgment against Baasha's royal house. Zimri wiped out all of Baasha's family and left no male heir alive.

versions.summary: Zimri was steward over King Elah's house in Tirzah, the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel. The title 'over the house' (Hebrew: al ha-bayit) was one of the highest administrative positions in the Israelite monarchy. It was in Zimri's house that King Elah was killed by Zimri, one of his commanders, while Elah was getting drunk. This event marked the end of Baasha's dynasty, fulfilling the words of the prophet Jehu. Zimri is mentioned only briefly in connection with this event in 1 Kings.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew title 'al ha-bayit' (על הבית), used for Zimri, means 'over the house'. This was one of the highest administrative positions in the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, comparable to a prime minister or chief steward. The title is also known from Assyrian and Egyptian parallels, where similar offices existed at royal courts.

Tirzah served as the capital of the northern kingdom from the division of the realm until Omri moved the capital to Samaria (around 880 BC). Archaeological excavations at Tell el-Far'ah (north) have uncovered remains of a significant Iron Age city, including a large palace complex that may have been the royal residence where Zimri and King Elah stayed.

Zimri's coup against Elah in Zimri's house is part of a pattern of political instability in the northern kingdom of Israel. Baasha's dynasty lasted only two generations, and Zimri himself reigned for just seven days before being overthrown by Omri. This constant shifting of dynasties in the northern kingdom contrasts with David's stable dynasty in Judah.

The fact that King Elah got drunk in his steward's house rather than in his own palace may indicate that the steward's residence was part of the royal palace complex in Tirzah, or that 'bayit' here refers to the administrative section of the court rather than a private dwelling.

The prophet Jehu son of Hanani had proclaimed judgment against Baasha's house because of Baasha's sins and his resemblance to the house of Jeroboam (1 Kings 16:1–4). The killing of Elah in Zimri's house was seen as a direct fulfillment of this prophecy, underscoring the Deuteronomistic historical view that kings' fates are tied to their obedience to God.
